A1.passage: Many people like cats. Some people are afraid of them.
Summer is hot. Some people love it, but others do not.
key_points: some love it, others do not

A1.passage: Big cities are exciting. Small towns are quiet and safe.
key_points: small towns are quiet and safe

A1.passage: Some students like tests. Many students feel nervous before tests.
Fast food is cheap, but it is not very healthy.
Many children want a pet. Pets need a lot of care.
Taking the train is slow, but you can read on it.
Some families eat dinner late. Others eat early.
Sports shoes are comfortable, but they can be expensive.
Rain is good for gardens, but it can make people sad.
Some people get up early. Others like to sleep late.
Hot food is nice in winter. Cold food is nice in summer.
My town has a new park. Some people want a shop there.
key_points: the town has a new park

A1.passage: Long walks are healthy, but some people have no time.
Many people buy flowers. Some say flowers cost too much.
Some children watch cartoons every day. Parents want them to read.
Cooking is fun, but cleaning the kitchen is not.
Some people sing in the car. Others want quiet.
Our school has a new computer room. Some teachers prefer books.
A big house is nice, but it is hard to clean.
Some workers wear a suit. Others wear jeans to work.
Snow is pretty, but it makes roads dangerous.
Many people like the beach. Some people prefer the mountains.
Buses are cheap, but they are often late.
Some children like school lunch. Others bring food from home.
An old bike is cheap. A new bike is safer.
Some people shop on Saturday. The shops are very busy then.
Birthday cakes are sweet and fun. Some people eat fruit instead.
Some people read on paper. Others read on a screen.
Playing games is fun, but too many games are bad.
Many people love chocolate. Doctors say eat only a little.
Some people drink tea with sugar. Others say sugar is bad for teeth.
A holiday by the sea is relaxing, but hotels are expensive.
Some people make their own bread. It takes a long time.
Taxis are fast, but they cost a lot of money.
Some children walk to school. Some parents think it is not safe.
Learning to drive is useful, but lessons are expensive.
Some people like hot showers. Cold showers wake you up.
Our class wants a trip to the zoo. Some students want the museum.
key_points: the class wants a zoo trip

A1.passage: Some offices have plants. Plants make people happy, but they need water.
Some people wear glasses. Others wear contact lenses.
Many people drive to work. Walking is better for health.

A2.passage: Many people now drink plant milk. They say it is healthier. Others think cow's milk tastes better.
Some schools give students tablets instead of books. They are light, but some students find screens tiring.
Our town wants a new car park. Drivers are happy, but some people want a playground.
key_points: a new car park is planned

A2.passage: Many young people use social media every day. It helps them keep in touch, but it wastes time.
key_points: social media keeps people in touch

A2.passage: Some families eat dinner in front of the TV. Others think meals are a time to talk.
key_points: some eat in front of the TV
meals are a time to talk

A2.passage: Many people now use electric toothbrushes. They clean well, but they are more expensive than normal ones.
Some workers listen to music at work. It helps them focus. Their managers think it is distracting.
Many hotels charge extra for breakfast. Some guests like to eat outside the hotel to save money.
key_points: guests eat outside to save money

A2.passage: Some teenagers get a job at sixteen. They learn about money, but they have less time for homework.
A new shopping centre will open outside town. Shoppers like it, but small shops in town may close.
Many people bring their own cups to cafes. Some cafes give them a small discount for this.
Some parents drive their children to every activity. Others think children should learn to take the bus.
key_points: children should learn to take the bus

A2.passage: Our office has a new coffee machine. Workers love it, but the coffee is not free.
Many people take photos of their food. They enjoy sharing them, but some friends find it boring.
Some cities have markets at night in summer. Visitors enjoy them, but residents complain about the noise.
Some children learn two languages at home. It is very useful, but it can be confusing at first.
key_points: it can be confusing at first

A2.passage: Many people now have a smart speaker at home. It is helpful, but some people worry it listens all the time.
Some students choose a university near home. It is cheaper. Others want to live somewhere new.
key_points: a university near home is cheaper

A2.passage: Many people celebrate birthdays at restaurants now. It is easy, but cooking at home is cheaper.
Some companies give workers free lunch every Friday. Workers enjoy eating together, but it costs a lot.
Many families have two cars. It is convenient, but cars are expensive to keep.
Some people buy a new phone every year. Others use the same phone for five years.
key_points: some buy a new phone yearly
others keep a phone for years

A2.passage: Our school will start a chess club. Some students are excited, but others want more sports clubs.
Some young people live with their parents until thirty. They save money, but they have less freedom.
Many airports now have shops and restaurants everywhere. Travellers like it, but prices are often very high.
Some people sleep with the window open. They like fresh air, but it can be cold and noisy.
key_points: it can be cold and noisy

A2.passage: More people are learning to play an instrument as adults. It is fun, but it needs a lot of practice.
Some cafes have board games for customers. Families enjoy them, but people stay a long time and buy little.
key_points: people stay long and buy little

A2.passage: Our neighbours want to cut down a big old tree. It blocks the light, but birds live in it.
Some people write shopping lists. They spend less. Others like to decide in the shop.
Many students study with music on. It helps them relax, but some teachers say it makes them slower.
Some towns have free concerts in the summer. Everyone can enjoy music, but the town pays for it.
Some people send handwritten letters at holidays. Others think a quick message is enough.
Many people now wear a watch that counts their steps. It helps them move more, but some feel stressed.
Some hairdressers are open late in the evening. Workers like this, but the staff go home very late.
Many people decorate their homes for holidays. It looks nice, but the lights use a lot of electricity.
key_points: lights use a lot of electricity

A2.passage: Some shops let customers return clothes for free. Shoppers like this, but the shops lose money.
Some people prefer to travel alone. They feel free. Others say travelling with friends is safer and more fun.
key_points: travelling with friends is safer and fun

A2.passage: Our town has a new bus app. Young people use it, but older people prefer paper timetables.
Many people now eat less meat. They say it is good for the planet. Others enjoy meat too much to stop.
key_points: eating less meat helps the planet

A2.passage: Some families share one computer. Children must wait, but parents can see what they do.
key_points: parents can see what they do

A2.passage: Some teachers let students use phones in class. It helps them look things up, but students may play games.
key_points: phones help students look things up

B1.passage: Many universities have stopped printing student handbooks and put all the information online. This saves paper and money, but some new students find important details hard to locate.
Several companies now give employees a budget to spend on training of their choice. Staff enjoy the freedom, though managers worry the courses will not match company needs.
key_points: courses may not match company needs

B1.passage: Some cities have started planting fruit trees in public parks so that anyone can pick the fruit. Residents like the idea, but cleaning up fallen fruit costs money.
A number of schools now invite local business people to teach short lessons about their jobs. Students learn about real careers, but some teachers say lessons are disrupted.
More families are swapping homes with other families for their holidays. It saves money on hotels, but some people are uncomfortable letting strangers stay in their house.
Some supermarkets now have a quiet hour each week for shoppers who need a calm environment. Many customers support the idea, while others find the timing inconvenient.
Many offices now turn off the heating on Fridays to save energy. Managers point to the lower bills, but staff who come in complain about the cold.
Some driving schools now teach lessons only in electric cars. Learners find them easier to drive, but they may struggle later with a manual car.
Several hospitals have started offering free parking for visitors. Families appreciate the help, but the hospitals lose income that paid for other services.
More young people are choosing to rent furniture rather than buy it. They can move easily, but over time renting can cost more than buying.
Some restaurants have removed prices from their menus and ask diners to pay what they think is fair. Some customers pay generously; others take advantage.
key_points: diners pay what they think is fair

B1.passage: A number of companies now hold meetings while walking outside. Employees say they feel more creative, though it is difficult to take notes or share documents.
key_points: hard to take notes or share documents

B1.passage: Some sports centres now let children under twelve use the facilities for free. Families welcome the change, but adult members worry about crowded halls.
Many town councils now send newsletters by email instead of by post. It is cheaper and faster, although older residents without internet may miss important news.
Some airlines let passengers pay extra to keep the seat next to them empty. Travellers enjoy the space, but others feel it makes flights more unequal.
key_points: pay to keep the next seat empty

B1.passage: Several schools have replaced their sports day races with team games so that every child can join in. Some parents agree, while others say competition is healthy.
More companies are hiring older people who have retired but want to work part-time. They bring experience, though some younger staff feel their chances of promotion are reduced.
Many tourist sites now sell tickets only online and in advance. Planning becomes easier, but visitors who arrive without booking are often turned away.
Some cinemas now offer reclining seats and meals served during the film. Many viewers love the comfort, but ticket prices have almost doubled.
A number of language schools now teach entirely through video lessons. Students can study anywhere, but they get less chance to practise speaking with others.
Some neighbourhoods organise monthly street parties where residents close the road and share food. People get to know their neighbours, but drivers must find another route.
key_points: neighbours get to know each other

B1.passage: Many cafes now charge extra for takeaway cups to reduce waste. Most customers accept the fee, but some feel they are being punished for being busy.
Some workplaces now provide nap rooms where staff can rest during the day. Supporters say short naps improve focus, while critics fear people will simply work longer hours.
A number of high schools have stopped giving prizes for top grades. They want to celebrate effort instead, but some high achievers feel their hard work is ignored.
Several towns have put pianos in train stations for anyone to play. Travellers often enjoy the music, but people waiting nearby sometimes complain about the noise.
More people are buying refurbished laptops instead of new ones. They are cheaper and reduce electronic waste, but buyers worry about batteries and short warranties.
Some hotels now offer late checkout until six in the evening. Guests enjoy the extra time, but cleaning staff struggle to prepare rooms for new arrivals.
Many students now use online flashcards to revise for exams. They are quick and convenient, but some teachers think students only memorise facts without understanding them.
Several clinics now send text reminders before every appointment. Fewer patients miss their visits, though some people find the frequent messages annoying.
Some offices have replaced meeting rooms for phone calls with small booths. Workers can talk without disturbing others, but the booths are often booked all day.
Many parents now track their teenagers' location with phone apps. They feel calmer knowing where their children are, but teenagers often feel they are not trusted.
Some local markets now let farmers sell directly to customers without any middlemen. Prices are fairer for farmers, but shoppers sometimes find fewer choices.
A number of employers allow staff to swap public holidays for other days. Employees can celebrate occasions that matter to them, but planning shifts becomes harder.
Some primary schools have started gardening lessons where children grow their own vegetables. Pupils enjoy being outside, but the lessons take time away from other subjects.
More people are using voice messages instead of typing texts. Speaking is faster, but listeners often find long voice messages annoying and hard to skip through.
Some apartment buildings now ban barbecues on balconies for safety reasons. Building managers say fires are a real risk, but residents feel they are losing a summer pleasure.
Many universities now offer exams that students can take at home. This reduces stress and travel, though some teachers worry that cheating is easier.
Several ski resorts are using artificial snow because winters have become warmer. This keeps businesses open, but making snow uses large amounts of water and energy.
key_points: uses lots of water and energy

B1.passage: Some workplaces encourage staff to take short breaks every hour to stretch. Employees feel healthier, but some managers think the breaks interrupt concentration.
Many bookshops now organise events where authors read from their new books. Readers enjoy meeting writers, but small shops struggle to cover the costs.
Some towns have started lending electric cars to residents by the hour. People can drive without owning a car, but the cars are not always available when needed.
key_points: electric cars rented by the hour
no need to own a car

B1.passage: Some theme parks now sell expensive passes that let visitors skip the queues. Those who pay save hours, but other visitors say the waiting becomes even longer.

B2.passage: Some governments are considering banning advertisements for high-interest loans. Supporters argue that vulnerable people would be protected from debt, while critics claim adults should be trusted to make their own financial decisions.
Several companies have started offering paid leave to employees who are moving house. It is seen as a sign of care, but some managers question whether it is necessary.
Many universities are being encouraged to replace exams with practical projects. Projects are believed to reflect real-world skills, although they are harder to mark fairly.
In some cities, landlords are no longer allowed to refuse tenants with pets. Pet owners welcome the change, but landlords worry about damage and higher repair costs.
More employers are offering mental health days in addition to normal sick leave. Supporters believe this reduces burnout, while some fear the days may be misused.
Several hospitals have introduced robots to deliver medicines and meals. Nurses gain more time for patients, but the robots are expensive and sometimes break down.
Some sports clubs are being asked to reduce ticket prices for young fans. If prices were lower, attendance might rise, but clubs fear losing important income.
A growing number of shops are refusing to accept returns of clothes that have been worn. Retailers say this prevents abuse, while customers feel it is too strict.
Some cities now require new buildings to include bird-friendly glass. Conservationists say thousands of birds would be saved each year, but developers complain about the extra cost.
Many companies are being urged to publish the gender balance of their leadership teams. Advocates say transparency drives change, while others argue that numbers alone tell little.
Some museums are considering opening late into the night once a week. Younger visitors would be attracted, but extra staff and security would be required.
Several schools have been allowed to use cameras in classrooms. Supporters say behaviour improves and teachers are protected, while critics argue that constant recording damages trust.
Many recruiters now check candidates' social media accounts before offering a job. Some see this as sensible research, but others believe private lives should not affect hiring decisions.
key_points: private life should not affect hiring

B2.passage: In several countries, plastic cutlery has been banned in restaurants and takeaways. Wooden alternatives are being used instead, although some customers complain they feel unpleasant to eat with.
Some employers have started paying staff weekly instead of monthly. Workers find budgeting easier, but payroll departments report that administration costs have increased.
More parents are choosing to educate their children at home. Supporters value the personalised attention, while critics worry that children may miss out on social development.
Many cities are considering lowering speed limits to thirty kilometres per hour in residential areas. Fewer serious accidents would occur, but drivers complain that journeys would take longer.
key_points: lower speed limits in residential areas

B2.passage: Several supermarkets have been asked to donate unsold food to charities instead of throwing it away. Waste would be reduced, but stores worry about the costs of storage and transport.
Some cities have been testing driverless buses on fixed routes. Supporters believe they could make public transport cheaper, though many passengers say they would not feel safe.
A number of universities now record whether students attend lectures, and low attendance may affect grades. Some say this encourages commitment, while others feel adults should choose.
Esports have been recognised as an official sport in some countries. Fans say players need real skill and discipline, but critics argue that sport should involve physical activity.
Many festivals have introduced cashless wristbands for all payments. Queues are shorter and theft is reduced, although visitors often lose track of how much they have spent.
Some councils are proposing to charge drivers for parking outside their own homes. The money would fund road repairs, but residents argue they already pay enough local tax.
Several countries have introduced a sugar limit for children's breakfast cereals. Health campaigners welcome the rule, whereas manufacturers say families should be free to decide.
More companies are offering employees shares in the business. If the company performs well, staff benefit directly; critics note, however, that workers also share the risk.
Some libraries have been redesigned as quiet co-working spaces for freelancers. This brings in new visitors, though traditional users complain that the atmosphere has changed.
Many hospitals have restricted visiting hours to give patients more rest. Doctors say recovery is faster, but families feel they are kept apart when they are needed most.
Several companies are piloting contracts in which pay is linked to measurable results rather than hours. Productive staff could earn more, but some fear constant pressure.
Some cities have been testing shorter green lights for pedestrians to keep cars moving. Drivers welcome the change, but older people say they cannot cross in time.
key_points: older people cannot cross in time

B2.passage: Many venues are limiting ticket resale to stop people selling at inflated prices. Fans support the idea, though some cannot resell tickets they are unable to use.
Some offices have removed bins from desks so that staff must use central recycling points. Recycling has improved, but employees find the change inconvenient.
In some regions, drivers over seventy must pass a test every few years to keep their licence. Supporters stress road safety, while older drivers feel unfairly targeted.
Some companies require new graduates to work in several departments during their first year. They gain a broad view of the business, but some would rather specialise immediately.
Many towns are allowing restaurants to place tables on pavements and in parking spaces. Streets feel livelier, but pedestrians and wheelchair users sometimes struggle to get past.
key_points: hard for pedestrians and wheelchair users

B2.passage: Several schools have been given funding to stay open in the evenings for community classes. Local people would benefit, but teachers worry about security and cleaning.
Online reviews are increasingly being used to choose doctors and dentists. Patients find them helpful, but professionals argue that reviews often reflect waiting times rather than medical quality.
Some employers have started offering childcare at the workplace. Parents find it much easier to return to work, though employees without children feel the benefit is unequal.
Several cities are banning wood-burning stoves to improve air quality. Health experts support the measure, while rural residents argue that stoves are an affordable source of heat.
Many football clubs are being encouraged to include fans on their boards. Supporters would have a real voice, but owners fear decisions could become slower.
Several retailers have extended their opening hours to midnight. Shoppers who work late appreciate the change, but employees are concerned about safety on late shifts.
Some universities have begun offering two-year degrees with shorter holidays. Students would save money and start work sooner, although the workload may become intense.
key_points: save money and start work sooner

B2.passage: Some public swimming pools have reduced the water temperature to save energy. Councils say costs must be cut, but regular swimmers, especially older ones, find the water too cold.

C1.passage: Libraries in several countries have begun eliminating late fees, arguing that fines deter the poorest readers from borrowing at all. Critics counter that without penalties, books are returned late or not at all, depriving other patrons.

Proponents of teaching philosophy in primary schools maintain that it sharpens reasoning and encourages respectful debate. Sceptics question whether young children can benefit from abstract discussion, and note that curricula are already overloaded with core subjects.

Employers increasingly hire on the basis of personality assessments rather than interviews alone. Advocates claim these tools reduce bias and predict job performance; critics argue that they reward conformity and can be easily gamed by well-prepared candidates.
key_points: reward conformity and can be gamed

C1.passage: Several cities have handed control of small public budgets directly to residents, who vote on local projects. Supporters believe this strengthens civic engagement, whereas sceptics note that participation is often low and dominated by already influential groups.
key_points: low participation dominated by influential groups

C1.passage: Advocates of a legal right to broadband argue that, since essential services increasingly operate online, connectivity has become as fundamental as electricity. Opponents contend that guaranteeing access in remote areas would impose prohibitive costs on providers and taxpayers.

Hospitals are increasingly using algorithms to prioritise patients in emergency departments. Supporters argue that triage becomes faster and more consistent, while clinicians caution that subtle symptoms may be overlooked when human judgement is sidelined.

Some legal experts propose that companies should be held liable for misinformation spread on their platforms. Supporters see this as long-overdue accountability; opponents fear it would encourage excessive censorship and stifle legitimate debate.

Some cities have begun requiring developers to include affordable units in every new residential project. Supporters argue this creates mixed communities, whereas developers warn that the obligation reduces profitability and may ultimately discourage construction altogether.
key_points: affordable units required in new housing

C1.passage: Proposals to extend the school day by an hour are often justified by the benefits of additional tutoring and supervised homework. Teachers' representatives, however, warn of burnout, and many parents value the afternoons for family time and extracurricular activities.
key_points: teacher burnout and lost family time

C1.passage: The practice of lending artworks between museums allows masterpieces to reach wider audiences. Conservators, however, increasingly argue that frequent transportation exposes fragile works to avoidable risk, and that high-resolution digital reproductions could satisfy much public curiosity.

Allowing students to grade one another's work is promoted as a way of developing critical judgement and reducing teachers' workload. Detractors argue that peer marking is often inconsistent and that friendships inevitably influence the scores awarded.
key_points: builds judgement and saves teacher time

C1.passage: Some economists argue that cities should scrap minimum parking requirements for new housing, freeing land for homes. Residents frequently object, fearing that competition for on-street spaces would intensify considerably.

Mandatory warning labels on alcoholic drinks, similar to those on cigarettes, have been proposed by health authorities. Supporters argue consumers deserve clear information about risks, whereas the industry insists such measures unfairly stigmatise moderate drinkers.

Some firms have abolished annual salary negotiations and instead set pay using transparent formulas based on role and experience. Proponents argue this eliminates gaps caused by negotiation skills; critics believe it discourages exceptional performance.

Rising numbers of patients are consulting chatbots before seeing a doctor. Proponents suggest this could relieve pressure on overstretched clinics, while medical professionals worry that inaccurate advice may delay treatment or cause unnecessary anxiety.

Historic city centres are often protected by strict planning rules that limit building height and design. Conservationists consider these essential, yet younger residents argue that such restrictions inflate housing costs and freeze cities in the past.

Several orchestras have adopted blind auditions, in which candidates perform behind a screen. Advocates credit the practice with reducing bias significantly; some musicians argue, however, that it ignores qualities such as stage presence and collaboration.

Wealthy football clubs increasingly own several teams in different countries, sharing players and expertise. Owners describe this as efficient global management, while fans of smaller clubs fear their teams are being reduced to feeder sides.

Proposals to make first aid training compulsory for all secondary school students have attracted widespread support. Critics do not dispute its value but question whether schools have adequate resources and qualified instructors to deliver it properly.
key_points: schools may lack resources and instructors

C1.passage: The growth of ghost kitchens, which prepare food exclusively for delivery, has lowered costs for restaurateurs. Critics argue that they hollow out high streets and offer poor working conditions, while consumers often have no idea where their meals are cooked.

Several universities now offer academic credit for internships and volunteering. Supporters regard this as recognition of valuable practical learning; sceptics question whether such experiences can be assessed rigorously, fearing degrees could lose academic credibility.
key_points: hard to assess and may weaken degrees

C1.passage: Employers are increasingly sponsoring staff to study for degrees in exchange for a commitment to remain with the company. Supporters see this as mutually beneficial, while critics argue such arrangements can trap employees in unsuitable roles.

The decline of local newspapers has prompted calls for public funding of community journalism. Advocates argue that local reporting is vital for holding councils accountable; opponents worry that state money could compromise editorial independence.

Some regions have restricted the construction of second homes, which often remain empty for much of the year. Supporters argue that local families are being priced out, whereas property owners maintain that they bring valuable spending to rural economies.

Recruiters in creative industries increasingly value portfolios of work over formal qualifications. This may open doors to self-taught talent, but critics note that building an impressive portfolio often requires unpaid time that many cannot afford.

Some cities have begun imposing a levy on vacant properties to discourage owners from leaving homes empty. Proponents expect more housing to become available; critics question whether the tax can be enforced fairly without intrusive inspections.

Mandatory continuing education for professionals such as accountants and engineers is intended to keep skills current. Many practitioners, however, regard the requirement as a box-ticking exercise, completing courses of limited relevance merely to retain their licence.

Organisers of major marathons have introduced lottery systems because demand vastly exceeds available places. Supporters consider lotteries the fairest approach, whereas experienced runners argue that qualifying times would better reward dedication and ability.

Researchers are developing crops engineered to withstand drought and disease. Proponents emphasise the potential to strengthen food security in a warming climate, while critics raise concerns about corporate control of seeds and long-term ecological effects.

Online marketplaces for handmade goods have given independent artisans access to global customers. However, many sellers complain that rising fees, intense competition and mass-produced items falsely labelled as handmade make it increasingly difficult to earn a living.

Proposals to replace printed textbooks entirely with digital resources promise lower costs and constantly updated content. Educators remain divided, however, as several studies suggest that students retain information more effectively when reading on paper.

Coastal towns threatened by rising seas face a stark choice between building costly defences and gradually relocating communities inland. Engineers favour flexible approaches, while residents are often deeply reluctant to abandon homes that families have occupied for generations.

Corporate mentoring schemes pairing junior staff with senior executives are widely praised for accelerating careers. Critics observe, however, that participation is often informal, meaning that those who already resemble senior leaders are disproportionately selected.

Restaurants that refuse bookings and operate first-come, first-served argue that this keeps tables full and treats all diners equally. Customers, however, frequently complain about long queues and the impossibility of planning special occasions.

Professional sports clubs increasingly schedule matches at late hours to suit international television audiences. Clubs value the broadcasting revenue, whereas local supporters complain that late kick-offs make attending in person impractical, especially for families.
key_points: hard for local fans and families

C1.passage: Platforms increasingly allow customers to rate individual delivery workers and drivers. Supporters argue that ratings maintain high standards; critics point out that workers can lose income because of factors beyond their control, such as traffic or customer bias.
key_points: workers penalised for things beyond control

C1.passage: The teaching of handwriting in an increasingly digital world is being questioned in several education systems. Proponents argue that writing by hand aids memory and fine motor development; opponents feel the time would be better spent on typing skills.

Several countries are investing in high-speed rail links intended to replace short-haul flights. Advocates highlight lower emissions and city-centre convenience, while sceptics question whether the enormous construction costs and decades-long timescales can be justified.

Accelerated learning programmes allow gifted children to skip school years. Supporters believe this prevents boredom and keeps talented pupils challenged, whereas critics warn that emotional maturity may lag behind, leaving children isolated among older classmates.

The use of drones for delivering parcels in residential areas promises faster service and reduced road traffic. Residents, however, have raised concerns about noise, privacy and safety, particularly over densely populated neighbourhoods and gardens.

Advocates of community energy schemes, in which residents jointly own local solar or wind installations, argue that they keep profits within communities. Sceptics doubt whether such projects can operate at sufficient scale to make a meaningful difference.
key_points: may be too small to matter

C1.passage: Shared parental leave policies allow both parents to divide time off after a child's birth. While the policy is widely praised, take-up among fathers remains low, with many citing career concerns and workplace culture as obstacles.
key_points: few fathers take it due to career and culture

C2.passage: Advocates of radical candour in workplaces maintain that unvarnished feedback accelerates growth and forestalls festering resentment. Detractors contend that, divorced from genuine rapport, such bluntness merely licenses cruelty, privileging the comfort of the speaker over the dignity of the recipient.

The ubiquity of chain cafes is lamented by some as an insidious homogenisation of urban life, eroding local distinctiveness. Others regard such lamentations as nostalgic snobbery, pointing out that standardisation offers reliability and affordability that many residents genuinely value.
key_points: they offer reliability and low prices

C2.passage: Proponents of degrowth argue that perpetual economic expansion is incompatible with ecological limits and that wealthy societies should deliberately reduce consumption. Critics dismiss the proposition as naive, warning that shrinking economies invariably inflict the greatest hardship on the most vulnerable.

Critics of the attention economy argue that applications engineered to maximise engagement exploit cognitive vulnerabilities, corroding users' capacity for sustained thought. Sceptics of this diagnosis counter that similar alarm accompanied the novel and television, and that moral panics routinely overestimate technology's influence.

The burgeoning practice of awarding honorary degrees to celebrities is defended as a means of raising institutional profiles. Purists deride it as a debasement of scholarly distinction, arguing that universities trade intellectual credibility for fleeting publicity.

Some ethicists argue that animals possessing demonstrable sentience should be accorded legal personhood, enabling advocates to sue on their behalf. Opponents caution that extending such status beyond humans risks diluting the concept and engendering considerable legal confusion.
key_points: dilutes the concept and causes confusion

C2.passage: Exponents of slow journalism argue that the relentless news cycle privileges immediacy over accuracy and comprehension, and advocate fewer, more thoroughly researched stories. Sceptics retort that such an approach is a luxury few outlets can afford, and that audiences demonstrably reward speed.
key_points: news cycle values speed over accuracy

C2.passage: The canonisation of certain novels as indispensable reading has been challenged as perpetuating a narrow conception of literary merit. Defenders of the canon maintain that its works endure precisely because they reward successive generations of readers, irrespective of fashion.
key_points: reflects a narrow idea of merit
classics endure because they reward readers

C2.passage: The professionalisation of youth sport, with children specialising intensively from an early age, is defended as the only route to elite performance. Physiologists and psychologists counter that early specialisation heightens injury risk and burnout, while varied play produces more resilient athletes.
key_points: seen as route to elite level

C2.passage: Advocates of the right to be forgotten maintain that individuals should be able to request the deletion of outdated personal information online. Opponents fear such provisions could be exploited to sanitise reputations and obstruct legitimate inquiry into past conduct.
key_points: right to delete old personal data

C2.passage: Grand infrastructure projects are notorious for exceeding their budgets, a tendency some attribute to systematic optimism among planners. Others argue that underestimation is strategic, since realistic forecasts would rarely secure approval, and that many landmarks would never have been built otherwise.

The resurgence of vinyl records and film photography is often attributed to a yearning for tangible, deliberate experiences amid digital abundance. Sceptics suggest that such revivals are less an authentic rejection of convenience than a marketable aesthetic adopted by affluent consumers.
key_points: really a fashionable aesthetic for the wealthy

C2.passage: The architectural preference for glass towers, once emblematic of corporate modernity, faces mounting criticism for their inefficiency in hot climates. Defenders contend that innovations in glazing mitigate such deficiencies, while critics argue that traditional local building methods offer more enduring solutions.
key_points: glass towers criticised in hot climates

C2.passage: Proponents of standardised international curricula praise their portability for globally mobile families and their rigorous benchmarks. Detractors argue that they marginalise local history and literature, cultivating a rootless elite more conversant with distant canons than with their own societies.
key_points: international curricula are portable and rigorous

C2.passage: Collectors and auction houses defend the lucrative market in antiquities as a means of preserving objects that might otherwise perish. Archaeologists counter that demand incentivises looting, and that artefacts severed from their original context forfeit much of their scholarly significance.
key_points: antiquities market claims to preserve objects

C2.passage: The prevalence of ghostwriting among public figures and executives raises questions about authenticity in published memoirs and opinion pieces. Some consider it an innocuous division of labour; others maintain that readers are entitled to know whose words they are actually reading.
key_points: readers deserve to know the author

C2.passage: Precision medicine, tailoring treatment to individuals' genetic profiles, promises unprecedented efficacy. Sceptics warn that its considerable costs could entrench disparities in healthcare, directing resources towards bespoke therapies for the affluent while basic provision for the many remains chronically underfunded.

Some philosophers maintain that wilderness should be valued intrinsically, irrespective of any benefit it confers upon humanity. Others, adopting a more pragmatic stance, contend that conservation succeeds only when framed in terms of tangible human interests such as clean water and livelihoods.

The ascendancy of the influencer as a cultural arbiter has democratised taste-making, wresting authority from critics and editors. Detractors lament the consequent blurring of advertising and opinion, while enthusiasts welcome the erosion of gatekeepers whose judgements were never as disinterested as they claimed.

Urban planners increasingly champion mixed-use zoning, interweaving housing, commerce and light industry. Critics caution that the resulting proximity breeds friction over noise and traffic, while advocates counter that the segregation of functions has produced sterile suburbs and interminable commutes.
key_points: separation caused dull suburbs and long commutes

C2.passage: Digital minimalism, the deliberate curtailment of one's technological engagement, is extolled as a remedy for distraction. Critics observe that the movement's prescriptions presuppose a degree of professional autonomy few enjoy, rendering it an individualised solution to what may be a structural predicament.

The anthropomorphic marketing of household robots invites users to form emotional attachments to machines. Some designers regard this as harmless, even comforting; ethicists caution that it exploits loneliness and obscures the commercial data collection that such companionship conveniently facilitates.
key_points: exploits loneliness and hides data collection

C2.passage: The enduring popularity of franchised television formats, replicated across dozens of countries, attests to their commercial efficacy. Cultural critics deplore the resulting monotony, whereas producers argue that local adaptations infuse borrowed templates with distinctly national sensibilities.

Exponents of evidence-based policy urge governments to trial interventions rigorously before implementing them nationwide. Critics argue that randomised trials are ill-suited to complex social problems, and that the insistence on proof can become a pretext for inaction.

The commodification of sleep, through costly mattresses, trackers and supplements, reflects heightened awareness of its importance. Detractors argue that the industry pathologises ordinary restlessness and markets expensive solutions to problems more plausibly attributable to excessive working hours and precarious employment.
key_points: real causes are long hours and insecurity

C2.passage: Proponents of cultivating national champions argue that governments should nurture strategically important firms through subsidies and protection. Free-market sceptics maintain that such favouritism breeds complacency, distorts competition and squanders public money on enterprises that markets have already judged uncompetitive.

The habit of posting preliminary research findings online before formal review has accelerated scientific exchange. Detractors caution that journalists frequently amplify unvetted conclusions, whereas proponents insist that transparency and rapid scrutiny by peers outweigh the hazards of premature dissemination.

The proliferation of exclusive members' clubs for professionals is portrayed by founders as fostering serendipitous collaboration. Critics suggest that such enclaves merely formalise networks of privilege, compounding advantages that already accrue to the well-connected.

The convention of awarding principal credit to lead investigators obscures the contributions of junior researchers and technicians. Reformers propose detailed contribution statements; traditionalists counter that such granular accounting would complicate evaluation without materially altering entrenched hierarchies.

The fashion for lavish destination weddings is defended as a personal prerogative. Detractors, however, decry the environmental toll of transporting guests across continents and the social pressure such events impose on friends and relatives of limited means.
key_points: destination weddings are a personal choice
pressure on guests with less money

C2.passage: The ascendancy of algorithmically generated playlists has transformed how listeners encounter music. Enthusiasts celebrate the effortless discovery of obscure artists; critics lament the decline of deliberate listening and the subtle pressure on musicians to compose for the algorithm's preferences.
key_points: less deliberate listening and pressure on musicians

C2.passage: The tenure system in academia is defended as the bulwark of intellectual freedom, enabling scholars to pursue unpopular inquiries without fear of dismissal. Critics contend that it shelters complacency and has fostered a precarious underclass of temporary lecturers bearing a disproportionate teaching burden.

The conception of childhood as a period requiring constant supervision has, some sociologists argue, deprived children of the unstructured independence through which resilience develops. Others maintain that heightened caution reflects legitimate responses to genuinely changed circumstances, such as heavier traffic.

Patrons of contemporary art increasingly treat acquisitions as speculative investments, storing works in warehouses rather than displaying them. Critics argue this transforms culture into an asset class divorced from public enjoyment; defenders claim such investment sustains a market upon which living artists depend.

The championing of resilience in education, teaching pupils to persevere through adversity, has been questioned by those who argue that it implicitly blames individuals for systemic failings. Proponents counter that cultivating perseverance equips young people for challenges no institutional reform can eliminate.

The vogue for immersive exhibitions, which project famous paintings onto vast walls accompanied by music, has drawn enormous crowds. Purists dismiss these spectacles as superficial entertainment; others regard them as a welcome gateway through which new audiences might discover original works.

Linguistic prescriptivists lament the erosion of grammatical conventions in informal digital communication. Descriptivists counter that language has always evolved through usage, and that today's perceived errors frequently become tomorrow's standard forms, rendering such lamentations futile.

The aspiration towards energy self-sufficiency, whereby nations generate all their power domestically, is championed as a safeguard against geopolitical volatility. Economists caution that such autarky sacrifices the efficiencies of trade and may ultimately raise costs for households and industry alike.
key_points: loses trade benefits and raises costs

C2.passage: The cult of busyness, in which perpetual occupation signals status, has drawn scrutiny from those who note that leisure was historically the marker of privilege. Critics contend that conspicuous overwork corrodes health and creativity, yet many professionals feel unable to resist it.

Exponents of open-source software argue that freely shared code produces more secure and innovative products through collective scrutiny. Sceptics observe that many critical projects depend on a handful of unpaid volunteers, rendering vital infrastructure precariously reliant on goodwill.
key_points: open code is secure and innovative

C2.passage: Proponents of rotating leadership, in which team members take turns directing projects, contend that it develops talent and diffuses entrenched hierarchies. Detractors suggest that the arrangement sacrifices continuity and accountability, as no individual retains ownership of long-term outcomes.

The cultivation of national dishes as emblems of identity frequently provokes disputes between neighbouring countries claiming the same recipes. Some regard these quarrels as harmless expressions of pride; others observe that culinary traditions have always circulated freely, rendering claims of exclusive ownership dubious.
